# Pie charts {#sec-pie-charts} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_koosh()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_koosh()`, built from a tri color Koosh ball: a white background, an orange frame, orange, purple, and black filament marks, peach and lilac accents, and an Arial Rounded title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pie_charts_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: :::: ## Description *“In general, pie charts work well when the goal is to emphasize simple fractions, such as one-half, one-third, or one-quarter.”* *“They also work well when we have very small datasets.”* - [Claus O. Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization (2019)](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/) Pie-charts are ideal for comparing the proportions of categorical variable values, and we can build pie-charts using the [`ggpubr` package.](https://rpkgs.datanovia.com/ggpubr/) ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} install.packages("ggpubr") library(ggpubr) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: The [Koosh ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koosh_ball) was a ball of rubber filaments that was easy to catch and impossible to bounce, and by the 90s it came in more styles than anyone needed. We'll simulate the styles of 200 Koosh balls sold at a toy store (tri color, rainbow, neon, and glow in the dark) with `sample()`. The probabilities are simple fractions on purpose: one half, one quarter, one eighth, and one eighth. Then we count each style (`cnt`) and convert the counts to proportions (`perc`). Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 200 Koosh balls every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1993) koosh_balls <- tibble( ball_id = 1:200, style = sample(c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow"), size = 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8))) koosh_pie <- koosh_balls |> count(style, name = "cnt") |> mutate( perc = cnt / sum(cnt), style = factor(style, levels = c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow"))) |> arrange(style) glimpse(koosh_pie) #> Rows: 4 #> Columns: 3 #> $ style Tri color, Rainbow, Neon, Glow #> $ cnt 98, 49, 23, 30 #> $ perc 0.490, 0.245, 0.115, 0.150 ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A pie chart is a whole cut into slices, so it only makes sense when the slices add up to one thing (here, 200 Koosh balls). Pie charts are easiest to read when the slices are simple fractions, and because we chose those fractions in `sample()`, we know what each slice should look like. Below we'll move from the Koosh balls, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first ten Koosh balls. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(koosh_balls$style, 10) #> [1] "Tri color" "Tri color" "Tri color" #> [4] "Rainbow" "Rainbow" "Rainbow" #> [7] "Tri color" "Tri color" "Glow" #> [10] "Tri color" ``` ::: ::: Counting all 200 and comparing each count to the count we'd expect (200 times each fraction) shows how close the simulation lands. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} koosh_pie |> mutate(expected = 200 * c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: A bar model lays the 200 Koosh balls out in a line. Tri color balls fill about half the bar, rainbow balls about a quarter, and neon and glow balls split the last quarter. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(data = koosh_pie, aes(x = cnt, y = "200 Koosh balls", fill = style)) + geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + geom_text(aes(label = cnt), color = "#FFFFFF", position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) + labs(x = "Koosh balls", y = NULL, fill = "Style") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pie_charts_files/figure-html/draw_bar_model_pie-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: A pie chart bends the same bar into a circle. Below, the pie on the left uses the exact fractions from `sample()`, and the pie on the right uses our simulated counts. The tri color slice covers about half the circle in both, and the rainbow slice covers about a quarter. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} expected_pie <- koosh_pie |> mutate(perc = c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8)) ggpubr::ggpie(expected_pie, x = "perc", label = paste0(round(100 * expected_pie$perc, 1), "%"), lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF", fill = "style", color = "white") + labs(title = "Expected", fill = NULL) + pie_theme ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie, x = "perc", label = paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc, 1), "%"), lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF", fill = "style", color = "white") + labs(title = "Simulated", fill = NULL) + pie_theme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pie_charts_files/figure-html/draw_pie-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pie_charts_files/figure-html/draw_pie-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each Koosh ball is one draw from four styles, so the four counts follow a [multinomial distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_distribution): $$ (N_{\text{tri color}}, N_{\text{rainbow}}, N_{\text{neon}}, N_{\text{glow}}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(200, \; \left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}\right)\right) $$ A slice's angle is its share of the 360 degrees in the circle: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is 180 degrees, $\tfrac{1}{4}$ is 90 degrees, and each $\tfrac{1}{8}$ is 45 degrees. Simple fractions like these line up with the "clock positions" our eyes already know (half past, quarter past), which is why pie charts work best with them. Each simulated share wobbles around its fraction by about $\sqrt{p(1 - p) / 200}$: about 3.5 percentage points for the tri color slice and 2.3 points for the neon and glow slices. That's why our slices are close to the expected ones but not exact. Try changing `size = 200` to `size = 20` in `sample()` and the slices drift much further from the simple fractions. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create the slice labels (`pie_labels`) with `paste0()` - `ggpie()` applies its own theme, so create `pie_theme` to add the book theme back (and remove the axis text, ticks, and grid lines) - Create labels with `labs()` - Assign the data to `ggpubr::ggpie()` - Assign `"perc"` to `x` - Assign `pie_labels` to `label` - Assign `"in"` to `lab.pos` - Assign a dark color to `lab.font` and `"white"` to `color` - Assign `"style"` to `fill` - Add `pie_theme` (which also moves the legend to the bottom) ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} pie_labels <- paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc), "%") pie_theme <- fmggp2::theme_koosh(base_size = 14) + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") labs_pie <- labs( title = "Koosh balls", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Styles sold at one toy store", fill = NULL) ggp2_pie <- ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie, x = "perc", label = pie_labels, lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF", fill = "style", color = "white") + pie_theme ggp2_pie + labs_pie ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pie_charts_files/figure-html/create_graph_pie-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: :::
